This analysis delves into the core selling points of SolidJS, including its impressive performance, fine-grained reactivity, and automatic dependency tracking. However, it also critically examines the significant trade-offs required to achieve this speed, such as the concept of 'vanishing components' that only run once and restrictions on prop destructuring.

summary:
## Is SolidJS Better Than React? This video provides a critical look at SolidJS, comparing its performance benefits against the significant trade-offs it makes, especially when contrasted with React. The author's conclusion is that for most developers and projects, **SolidJS is not a better choice than React**. While its speed is impressive, the cost of learning a new, subtly different mental model and leaving React's vast ecosystem is too high. ### Key Selling Points of SolidJS * **Performance**: SolidJS is demonstrably faster than React, which is its primary selling point. It achieves this through a different compilation and reactivity strategy. * **Familiar Syntax**: It uses JSX and a component-based architecture, making it look and feel familiar to React developers at a surface level. * **Fine-Grained Reactivity**: It implements a reactivity system similar to MobX or Vue, where dependencies are tracked automatically. This means you don't need manual dependency arrays like in React's `useEffect`. ### The Trade-Offs and "Gotchas" SolidJS's speed comes from a set of design choices that create a different mental model from React. The author compares learning it to **riding a bike with reversed handlebars**—it's familiar enough to be confusing because your instincts are wrong. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Components Only Run Once**: Unlike React, a SolidJS component function is executed only a single time. It is not re-run on updates. All logic that needs to react to state changes must be placed inside reactive primitives (like JSX expressions, effects, or memos). This leads to several critical rules you must follow: * **Accessing State**: State from a signal must be accessed as a function call (e.g., `count()`) to register the dependency. * **No Prop Destructuring**: Destructuring the `props` object (e.g., `const { name } = props;`) will break reactivity because Solid tracks property access on the `props` object itself. You must always use `props.name`. > [!TIP] > To handle conditional logic or derived values that need to be reactive, you must use one of these patterns: > * Place the logic directly inside the JSX: `
{props.value || 'default'}
` > * Wrap it in a helper function: `const A = () => props.value || 'default'` > * Use a dedicated primitive like `createMemo` for expensive computations. ### Final Verdict For 99% of use cases, the author argues that the performance of React is **perfectly fine**. The benefits of React's mature ecosystem, community support, and the developer's existing familiarity far outweigh the raw speed advantage offered by SolidJS. The cognitive overhead of retraining your brain to avoid common React patterns makes the switch difficult and potentially error-prone.

## It Depends, But For Me, It's No

Solid.js is not exactly a new framework because it says it's been in development for five years, but it definitely seems to have the newest buzz around it. And the question inevitably becomes, is it better than my favorite framework? Is Solid.js better than React? Is it better than Vue.js? Is it better than Angular? Is it better than jQuery?

The answer may surprise you. So, rather than you wait until the end of the video for the answer, I'm just going to tell you now, and then you can just stop watching and just have a tuna fish sandwich because I know that's what you're craving right now. The answer to 'Is Solid.js better than your favorite framework?' is: it depends. I know, I know. I'm not supposed to say that. I'm supposed to say something that like, yes, it's better, or no, it's not as good. But honestly, with everything in technology, as you have been around for longer, the answer almost always inevitably is 'it depends.'

There are a few times where you can say, yes, Solid.js is better than jQuery, but also it depends. Are you just trying to add an event handler across every browser? Then jQuery is fine. Are you trying to make a web application? Then Solid.js is definitely better. But today, I'm going to really delve into is Solid.js better than React? And the answer is largely no.

In my opinion, SolidJS is not better than React, but also it does depend because it kind of changes depending upon what you're valuing more. Are you putting a premium on speed and size of your code? Then Solid.js is probably going to be a little bit better than React. But is that worth the trade-off to the mountains and years of community and history that exists with React.js? Probably not. So let's delve in together with Solid.js to kind of understand why I'm not that bullish on Solid.js. But again, it depends, but also no, it's not for me.

## First Impressions & The Performance Pitch

So right away, Solid.js's web page is better than React's, in my opinion. That's it, video over. I like the web page better. It's a little bit happier and, you know, it really behooves them to make a better website because they definitely have to kind of persuade you to use Solid.js over React. Yes, why change everything and try something new and experimental when React.js is tried and true, just that stallion that can ride into the sunset forever?

The big selling point of Solid.js, I think, is two things. One, it's similar to React in the sense that it uses JSX and components and kind of cribs similar APIs to hooks. But the big selling point by far is that it's faster than React. So sure, if that's your target you want to go after, then Solid.js is the thing to do.

They have this nice little graph here that shows that it is super fast, but like, are your users going to care that React is 1.93 times compared to 1.05? I don't even know what the denominator time... oh, time. So it's almost twice as fast. I don't know how to do math, I'm not a mathematician, just a developer. But do people care that Solid.js is faster than React by that much? Like, is that going to impact things? Maybe for some applications, but by and large, no. And again, you know, Solid.js has a huge uphill battle against it, and I do empathize with that because it's so hard to kind of usurp the crowning king. And, you know, it has all the features that people love and expect from a React.js framework.

## The Three Core Concepts of SolidJS

But this Get Started page is kind of where I'm going to spend most of my time today, where it kind of just explains how Solid.js behaves. And I think this is where I start falling off the bandwagon.

Solid.js, to accomplish its main goal of being super fast, makes different trade-offs to React that require learning how to do. And if you're coming from React or any other framework, you're going to have to spend some time, like anything, to learn things. And like, it just takes time. Do you want to spend that time on this framework that is new and not widely used? Or are you going to use what you already have with React? I mean, I wouldn't use Solid.js in a production application, but for my fun little side project, I think it's fine.

So in the Getting Started, it makes sure that Solid.js looks nice and familiar with components, and that's fine. And it talks about this `createSignal`, which, you know, doesn't look that dissimilar from React's `useState`, and that's fine too. And it kind of starts trying to tease you into thinking about Solid. I mean, to its credit, SolidJS does a great job with its Getting Started introduction to kind of ease you into the way of thinking in the Solid.js world.

The three main ideas here are declarative data, which is different than declarative UI, so that's kind of fun, but you can kind of declare your data. Vanishing components. I don't like this. This is probably the biggest thing that kind of hurts my head, frankly, of all the things in Solid.js, but we'll talk about it. And then read/write segregation, so that things are predictable. And I like this actually: 'Simple is better than easy.' I love these small first things. The things that 'simple is better than easy.' It's better to make things simple so that you can understand it, and you know, at that cost of making things maybe a little bit more difficult but still simple.

## Fine-Grained Reactivity and Automatic Tracking

And so let's talk about reactivity. And this is actually one of the things that I do love about Solid.js. It takes a similar approach to MobX or Vue. I am a huge fan of MobX; if I used Vue more, I probably would be as well. I do love Vue the little amounts of times that I play with it. But what's really cool about the MobX way and Vue way of doing things is that it has... dependencies are automatically tracked. And this is just really, really cool. It means there's no need for you as the developer to kind of tell your application, the framework like React or something, when things change and when you should update things. It's just built in.

And the way that it does things is with this `createSignal`, kind of like `useState`. This is the state, so you can reference it through a function. You can then set it through a setter. And essentially, whenever you call `setState`, it's telling Solid.js to re-update things. And again, this doesn't look that different from React, but how it's being implemented under the hood is where things kind of diverge and really hurts me. And it's also why the state is being invoked as a function, that's another thing.

Where we keep going, keep going, keep going. I just, I just want to get this whole idea here. It tells you about how signals work. They're essentially event emitters that hold a list of subscriptions, which is fine. And then here is a section about the trade-offs that Solid.js must do for this automatic dependency tracking to take effect.

## The Trade-Offs: Vanishing Components and Prop Rules

All reactivity is tracked through function calls, which is fine. You can... In React, if you call `setState` and all that stuff, it's hidden. Beneath, in Solid.js, it's beneath getters and proxies, which means that when you access properties is important. I'll get to it in a second.

Components are only executed once, which again, this is the thing that kind of kills me. Such a mental shift in the way of doing things. Destructuring or logic top-level in your components will not re-execute, and that means that you must access these things within other reactive parts of your codebase to make sure that things are re-evaluated. And these things are only tracked synchronously, so if you have a `setTimeout`... and I'm sure there's workarounds, I mean, they're all workarounds, they have a whole list of them. But again, trade-offs. What do you, what do you want to do?

So rendering kind of talks about JSX, how things work. You don't have to use `class`, and you can use `class`, that's fine. You can add properties. The entry point has to be a function. You have components where you can pass in properties, just like React and JSX, that's nice and fun. You have a signal where you're passing a prop through, you know, you're invoking the function to get the value down there.

And then here's where it's talking about destructuring. So here's a component, a component that has props given to it. And Solid.js makes an important note that you cannot use object destructuring on the props of an object. This is because behind the scenes, the way that Solid.js tracks usage is based off access off of that object. So for example, you have to call the property off of the object. This will not work. It will not update. It is not reactive because it is destructured into `name`. So that's a fine thing to remember forever in your Solid.js applications.

And then this is the thing that's really wild to me, is that Solid function components are only executed once rather than every render cycle. And I'm pretty sure that's why Solid.js is faster. Like, I'm sure it is. You only have to call functions once. That's a huge win in terms of just overhead, by and large.

## The "Reversed Handlebars" Problem

But it really forces you then to kind of rethink how you do things entirely. In React, I'm very used to doing this, where if, you know, value is undefined, the value will default to `default`. But with Solid.js, this is only called once. So depending upon what the value of this is will decide that rendered UI for all time. So instead, the workaround here is to put the behavior where Solid.js can observe it. So in this case, Solid.js does observe JSX. So if you put it just in line, then that'll work every time. It'll call that.

You can hoist that into a function, just like you do with the `createSignal`. And then you can also use `createMemo`. And then, as I mentioned, there's helpers to merge props here, which is nice and fun. But again, as a reminder, this bad. Bad. Don't do this. You must do things correctly. And there's also other prop helpers, `mergeProps`, `cloneProps`, all these things here. And like, that's a big change in how you do things, how you have to think about how things work.

There's already gotchas with React. React is by far no saint when it comes to gotchas, but you've been potentially developing with React for a long time now and are used to them. You already are aware of the pitfalls that React has and are pretty able to sidestep them and not step into them. What's hard about here with Solid.js is that it's just enough like React.js that it's like learning how to ride a bike with the front wheels turned backwards. Like if you flip the front wheels 180... I've never seen this video on YouTube. This is on YouTube, right? Yeah, it's on YouTube, where somebody has to learn how to ride a bike where everything's the same except the front wheel is just turned 180. And it's near impossible, if you... I don't know what you Google. It's like some YouTube video, 'bike front wheel backwards.' But this is kind of what it feels like here, where Solid.js has done a lot of effort, a lot of work to make it look as close and familiar to React.js as possible. But there's this fundamental difference in how things work. The front handlebars have been turned around such that all your instincts are going to be fighting against yourselves, where you're not going to think about... you're going to structure things by default because that's what you're used to. You're going to just call the value without invoking a function to get the value. You're not going to think about calling these, all these different things. You have to kind of just retrain your mind, which is going to be awkward, I imagine.

## Final Verdict: Why I'm Not Switching

And again, I'm projecting. I have not taken the time to use Solid.js. You are welcome to change my mind if you have used it extensively, but this is where I get a little bit more cautious about it. I think it's, I think it's really cool. I think it's really exciting, but it's definitely not free. Nothing's free. But this is also, again, a little bit weird in terms of like what you're going to actually have to do with it.

So that's the deal. Like, you know, is Solid.js better than React? For me, no. Do you want things to be super, super, super fast? Then yeah, it's better. But I think for 9.9 times out of 10, React is fine. We're not making rocket science applications, unless you work for a space company. And if you are, then again, do you need things to be that much faster? Wouldn't you rather have some environment that you're used to working with? You know the gotchas there that you can look out for than having to kind of just retrain your brain to steer backwards? It just seems hard.

And, you know, I don't like putting other things down because I do like to have things tried out. But for me, that's really why I'm not going to spend more time trying out Solid.js. I don't really see the immediate value that I'll get from learning how to do things here. I do not need the additional speed burst that Solid.js is really banking on. I think the ideas in Solid.js are really cool. I think that's definitely, I think that could be stolen from other frameworks, React or something else, but I doubt it will be. But is it worth the trade-offs? No, not for me.

## Will I Change My Mind?

I'd be curious to hear your thoughts. I'd love for you to change my mind. I will happily listen to all your arguments and read them and kind of think about what you have to say, because I love having my mind changed.

What have I changed my mind recently? I was talking to friends about mint chocolate chip ice cream, and I think it's disgusting because why do you want mint in your ice cream? Just use mint in either toothpaste or mojitos, that's it. But I will say, last time I tried mint chocolate chip ice cream, I was probably like 15 and just a naive adolescent. So it is bygone for me to try it again. So I will report back after I tried mint chocolate chip if my taste buds have changed, and I will change my mind on mint chocolate chip. So stay tuned for that riveting update, I'm sure.

But in terms of Solid.js, do change my mind. I want to hear more details about it and learn about it more. But from what I've read so far, without taking too much time towards studying it intensely, not for me.
